title: On-demand usage
prompt: Choose the one correct statement about the on-demand concept.

choices.text: Request resources when needed and review capacity based on usage.
choices.explanation: This describes the ability to use resources when they are needed.

choices.text: You must always purchase the maximum number of instances needed several years in the future before you begin using them.
choices.explanation: Pre-purchasing the maximum number of instances is not a feature of on-demand usage.

choices.text: Costs will always be minimized even if you do not check usage.
choices.explanation: To keep costs down, you need to review usage.

source.label: AWS: Six advantages of cloud computing

learning.reason: This describes the ability to use resources when they are needed.
learning.concept: Explain why usage should be adjusted based on on-demand access and pay-as-you-go pricing.

title: Costs That Remain After Stopping
prompt: You stopped the compute processing and kept the result data and disks. Choose the one judgment that is incorrect.

choices.text: Check the charges for stored resources too.
choices.explanation: Compute and storage are different cost factors.

choices.text: Because compute has been stopped, the costs of all related resources will always be zero.
choices.explanation: Stopping compute alone does not necessarily eliminate the costs of the storage resources you kept.

choices.text: Separate the data needed to resume from resources that are no longer needed.
choices.explanation: Checking why you are keeping resources helps clarify both costs and the requirements for resuming.

source.label: AWS: Six Advantages of Cloud Computing

learning.reason: Stopping compute alone does not necessarily eliminate the costs of the storage resources you kept.
learning.concept: Explain why it is useful to adjust usage based on on-demand pricing and pay-as-you-go billing.

title: Workload That Increases Only at Month-End
prompt: Choose 2 correct responses to handling an environment where processing volume increases only at month-end.

choices.text: Measure typical usage and start with the amount needed.
choices.explanation: Measurement provides a basis for capacity adjustment decisions.

choices.text: After processing is complete, reduce the added compute resources.
choices.explanation: When usage falls, restoring capacity reduces unnecessary operation.

choices.text: It is essential to always run all resources at maximum capacity.
choices.explanation: With on-demand usage, it is not necessary to maintain maximum capacity at all times.

choices.text: If you use the cloud, there is no need to check automatic adjustment conditions.
choices.explanation: When automating, check the conditions and limits as well.

choices.text: There are no costs whatsoever for storage or data transfer.
choices.explanation: Check cost factors beyond compute as well.

source.label: AWS: Six Advantages of Cloud Computing

learning.reason: Measurement provides a basis for capacity adjustment decisions.
learning.concept: Explain why usage should be adjusted based on on-demand usage and pay-as-you-go pricing.

title: Shared Responsibility
prompt: Choose one item that AWS is responsible for.

choices.text: The scope of data access selected by the user
choices.explanation: Users set and verify the scope of data access.

choices.text: Physical security of AWS facilities
choices.explanation: This is AWS's responsibility for the physical infrastructure it manages.

choices.text: Updates to the guest OS installed by the user
choices.explanation: Updates to the guest OS managed by EC2 users are the user's responsibility.

learning.reason: This is AWS's responsibility for the physical infrastructure it manages.
learning.concept: Determine whether AWS or the user is responsible based on the service used and the layer being managed.

title: EC2 OS Updates
prompt: When the EC2 guest OS needs an update, select the one incorrect judgment.

choices.text: Plan updates and verify operation on the customer side.
choices.explanation: This is a measure for the guest OS managed by the customer.

choices.text: Security measures for AWS facilities and OS updates are managed at different layers.
choices.explanation: The physical infrastructure and the guest OS have different areas of responsibility.

choices.text: Because the OS runs on AWS, the customer does not need to consider updates.
choices.explanation: Updating the EC2 guest OS remains the customer's responsibility.

learning.reason: Updating the EC2 guest OS remains the customer's responsibility.
learning.concept: Determine AWS's and the customer's responsibilities based on the service used and the layer each manages.

title: Responsibilities That Remain Even with Managed Services
prompt: Select two statements about the shared responsibility model that are incorrect.

choices.text: The scope of the customer's operational responsibilities varies by service.
choices.explanation: The layers you delegate differ from one service to another.

choices.text: With S3, the customer is responsible for checking access permissions for stored data.
choices.explanation: Even when you delegate infrastructure operations, the customer still manages data permissions.

choices.text: With managed services, customers no longer need to configure any security settings.
choices.explanation: Responsibilities such as managing data and access permissions remain.

choices.text: Updating the EC2 guest OS is the same responsibility as managing physical access to AWS facilities.
choices.explanation: The customer updates the guest OS; AWS manages the physical security of its facilities.

choices.text: Determine responsibility by checking the service in use and the layer in question.
choices.explanation: Identify the boundary instead of treating everything as one responsibility.

learning.reason: Responsibilities such as managing data and access permissions remain.
learning.concept: Determine which responsibilities belong to AWS and the customer based on the service in use and the layer being managed.

title: Region and AZ
prompt: Choose the one incorrect statement about Regions and AZs.

choices.text: An AZ is an isolated location within a Region.
choices.explanation: AZs are located within a Region.

choices.text: One AZ is a geographic unit that groups multiple Regions together.
choices.explanation: The hierarchy is reversed. AZs are located within a Region.

choices.text: A Region is a geographic unit for deploying resources.
choices.explanation: Select a Region to deploy resources.

learning.reason: The hierarchy is reversed. AZs are located within a Region.
learning.concept: Explain the Region/AZ hierarchy and shared failure scope.

title: Shared failure domain
prompt: You’re checking two servers in the same AZ. Select the two correct statements.

choices.text: It may provide protection against the failure of one server.
choices.explanation: The scope of a single-server failure differs from that of an AZ-wide outage.

choices.text: Both servers may be affected by an AZ-wide outage.
choices.explanation: They share the same failure domain: the AZ.

choices.text: Having two servers does not guarantee immunity to an AZ outage.
choices.explanation: The number of servers alone cannot separate them into different failure domains.

choices.text: Adding AZs alone does not automatically replicate all data to another Region.
choices.explanation: Replication to another Region requires service-specific configuration and operation.

choices.text: Using the Region selector moves existing servers to another Region.
choices.explanation: Changing the Region shown does not move resources.

learning.reason: The scope of a single-server failure differs from that of an AZ-wide outage.
learning.concept: Explain the Region/AZ hierarchy and shared failure domains.

title: Post-distribution checks
prompt: Choose the two statements that are incorrect judgments after placing workloads in different AZs.

choices.text: Check whether traffic flows to the healthy processing target.
choices.explanation: Both placement and the communication path are necessary.

choices.text: Check whether data can still be accessed when one AZ is unavailable.
choices.explanation: Processing cannot continue if the required data is unavailable.

choices.text: Since placement has been split, there is no need to check the capacity of the remaining resources.
choices.explanation: Check the remaining capacity during a failure.

choices.text: If multiple AZs are used, replication to another Region must also be complete.
choices.explanation: Distribution across AZs and replication to another Region are not the same.

choices.text: Explain which failures the design prepares for by looking at placement and dependencies.
choices.explanation: This helps clarify the scope of failures, which cannot be determined from the number of instances alone.

learning.reason: Check the remaining capacity during a failure.
learning.concept: Explain the Region/AZ hierarchy and shared failure domains.

title: Availability decisions
prompt: Choose the most appropriate first question to ask when considering availability.

choices.text: Who would be affected by an outage, and how long could they wait?
choices.explanation: The impact of an outage and the required continuity are the starting points for design.

choices.text: Should you maximize the number of instances regardless of the purpose of the configuration?
choices.explanation: The number of instances alone does not indicate what is needed or the scope of a failure.

choices.text: If you use the cloud, is it unnecessary to assess the impact of an outage?
choices.explanation: You still need to assess the impact of an outage in the cloud.

learning.reason: The impact of an outage and the required continuity are the starting points for design.
learning.concept: Compare configurations by distinguishing among workload, failure, and cost.

title: Comparing Instance Count and Placement
prompt: Plan A has 3 instances in AZ-a, while Plan B has 1 instance each in AZ-a and AZ-b. Select the 2 correct comparisons for a failure that takes AZ-a offline.

choices.text: All 3 instances in Plan A go down.
choices.explanation: Because all 3 instances are in the same AZ-a, they share AZ-a’s failure domain.

choices.text: Plan B retains 1 instance in AZ-b, but check whether that instance can handle the required workload.
choices.explanation: Because the instances are distributed across AZ-a and AZ-b, 1 instance remains, but its remaining capacity must be checked separately.

choices.text: Plan A has more instances, so at least 1 remains after an AZ-a failure.
choices.explanation: Because all 3 instances are in AZ-a, they all go down if AZ-a fails.

choices.text: Plan B retains 1 instance in AZ-b, so there is no need to check whether it can handle the required workload.
choices.explanation: Even if 1 instance remains, you still need to check whether it can handle the required workload.

choices.text: All configurations cost the same, so there is no need to compare them.
choices.explanation: Compare the costs of the additional resources and operations as well.

learning.reason: The number of instances alone does not determine processing capacity.
learning.concept: Compare configurations by distinguishing workload, failures, and cost.

title: Distinguishing load from failures
prompt: Select the two statements about load mitigation and failure mitigation that are incorrect.

choices.text: Treat handling congestion and preparing for an AZ failure as separate concerns.
choices.explanation: Capacity and failure scope serve different purposes.

choices.text: Increasing processing capacity also prevents AZ failures, regardless of placement.
choices.explanation: Increasing capacity may still leave a shared failure domain.

choices.text: With multiple AZs, there is no need to consider operational burden or cost.
choices.explanation: Also account for the added burden of increased resources and operations.

choices.text: Compare configurations by putting the remaining risks into words.
choices.explanation: Knowing what is prevented and what remains helps with decision-making.

choices.text: An outage may have different impacts on a learning system and an order intake system.
choices.explanation: The continuity required depends on the use case.

learning.reason: Increasing capacity may still leave a shared failure domain.
learning.concept: Compare configurations by distinguishing load, failures, and cost.

title: EC2’s role
prompt: Choose one correct statement about EC2.

choices.text: A virtual server that lets users manage the operating system and applications.
choices.explanation: With EC2, users choose the operating system and manage applications and updates.

choices.text: A function that runs code only when a file arrives.
choices.explanation: This describes Lambda.

choices.text: A bucket that stores objects under keys.
choices.explanation: This describes S3.

learning.reason: Understand EC2 in terms of how much of the runtime environment users manage.
learning.concept: EC2 is a virtual server.

title: Lambda Triggers
prompt: I want to run image resizing only when an image arrives in S3. Choose one suitable execution approach to consider first.

choices.text: Keep monitoring solely with an always-on EC2 instance.
choices.explanation: Even if this configuration is possible, first consider why continuous monitoring would be necessary when the requirement is to process only arrival events.

choices.text: Invoke Lambda on an S3 object creation event.
choices.explanation: This meets the requirement by running a short task in response to an event.

choices.text: Use S3 as a database and run SQL aggregations.
choices.explanation: S3 is for file storage, not an execution approach for image resizing.

learning.reason: Connect the trigger to the execution approach.
learning.concept: Lambda is event-driven.

title: Choosing an execution model
prompt: You want dedicated software to run continuously on an OS, and you also want to manage when OS patches are applied. Choose the most appropriate decision.

choices.text: Compare EC2 after checking the trigger for execution, processing time, and whether OS management is required.
choices.explanation: Because continuously running software and OS management by the user are requirements, these are factors for comparing EC2.

choices.text: Do not use the need for OS management as a factor when choosing an execution model.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Who manages the OS is important when comparing EC2 and Lambda.

choices.text: With Lambda, users can keep any OS service running and manage it themselves.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Lambda is not a virtual server where users operate the OS.

learning.reason: Choose based on both the requirements and management responsibilities.
learning.concept: Managing a continuously running OS is not an assumption of Lambda.

title: S3 Units
prompt: Choose one incorrect statement about S3.

choices.text: Objects are handled using keys within a bucket.
choices.explanation: In S3, objects are identified by keys.

choices.text: Connect it to EC2 and use it as an operating system block device.
choices.explanation: This is how EBS is used, so it is incorrect as a description of S3.

choices.text: You can store objects such as images and documents.
choices.explanation: S3 is object storage.

learning.reason: Distinguish objects from attached disks.
learning.concept: S3 is object storage.

title: Choosing a storage destination
prompt: Choose the one incorrect description of a storage destination for the file system used by an EC2 operating system.

choices.text: Choose only S3 as a disk attached to EC2.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Consider EBS when you need an attached disk.

choices.text: Consider EBS as block storage attached to EC2.
choices.explanation: This is suitable for use as an operating system file system.

choices.text: Consider S3 for uploaded PDFs, which are handled by key.
choices.explanation: This is suitable for storing and retrieving files as objects.

learning.reason: Choose a storage destination based on how the data will be used.
learning.concept: EBS is block storage for EC2.

title: Separation of storage
prompt: For a design that separates the photos themselves from the EC2 operating system area, choose one incorrect statement.

choices.text: The photos themselves can be handled as S3 objects.
choices.explanation: You can use S3 to store and retrieve photos by key.

choices.text: You can consider EBS attached to EC2 for the operating system area.
choices.explanation: Consider EBS as the disk used by the operating system.

choices.text: Store everything in IAM, even when the items being stored are different.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. IAM provides access control; it is not a storage destination.

learning.reason: Avoid confusing the responsibilities of different services.
learning.concept: IAM is not a storage service.

title: RDS and DynamoDB
prompt: Choose the two correct statements about RDS and DynamoDB.

choices.text: RDS is a candidate for data that uses table relationships and SQL.
choices.explanation: RDS is a service for running relational databases.

choices.text: DynamoDB automatically optimizes any kind of query afterward.
choices.explanation: You need to design the keys you will access in advance.

choices.text: DynamoDB is a service for attaching OS disks.
choices.explanation: OS disks are provided by EBS.

choices.text: With DynamoDB, start your design with the keys you will read and write.
choices.explanation: Think through key-centered access patterns first.

choices.text: RDS is a service for storing files using object keys.
choices.explanation: This describes S3.

learning.reason: How you query the data influences your choice.
learning.concept: RDS centers on relationships; DynamoDB centers on keys.

title: Order Data Decisions
prompt: I want to join customers, orders, and order line items, then aggregate the data monthly. Select 2 correct decisions.

choices.text: There is no need to consider data relationships, so consider only storage.
choices.explanation: Because joining and aggregation are required, review the relationships and query requirements.

choices.text: Compare RDS because SQL joins and aggregation are needed.
choices.explanation: It addresses requirements centered on queries across related data.

choices.text: Choosing S3 eliminates the need to join order tables.
choices.explanation: S3 is object storage and does not address the required joins.

choices.text: Choosing EC2 eliminates the need to decide on a data model.
choices.explanation: Choosing a compute approach does not remove the need to design data queries.

choices.text: Choose a database after reviewing the required queries and consistency needs.
choices.explanation: Compare services based on requirements, not their names.

learning.reason: Use query requirements as a selection criterion.
learning.concept: Joins and aggregation are factors to consider when comparing RDS.

title: Access patterns
prompt: Choose 2 correct principles to consider before selecting DynamoDB.

choices.text: Write down in advance which keys you will use to read and write.
choices.explanation: Design access patterns around keys.

choices.text: Assume that any columns can be joined later without limit.
choices.explanation: Do not assume relational joins.

choices.text: Check whether the required queries align with key access.
choices.explanation: Compare the requirements with the data model.

choices.text: Apply OS patches to DynamoDB.
choices.explanation: Databases are not subject to OS management.

choices.text: Use an S3 bucket for SQL joins instead of DynamoDB.
choices.explanation: S3 is not a relational database for SQL joins.

source.label: Best practices for designing and using partition keys

learning.reason: Check that keys align with queries.
learning.concept: Design DynamoDB based on access patterns.

title: Separation of responsibilities
prompt: Select two incorrect statements about designing CSV ingestion, content inspection, business data registration, and source file storage.

choices.text: Store the original CSV in S3.
choices.explanation: This fits the role of storing files as objects.

choices.text: Use IAM as the storage destination for CSV contents.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. IAM provides access control; it is not a data storage destination.

choices.text: Choose how to run the inspection process based on the event and the processing required.
choices.explanation: Check whether the process needs to run at the time of input, then choose an approach.

choices.text: If you choose EC2, you do not need to consider the database query requirements.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Compute and database decisions are separate.

choices.text: Register business data in a database suited to the queries required.
choices.explanation: Compare RDS and DynamoDB based on query and relationship requirements.

learning.reason: Design the architecture without mixing responsibilities.
learning.concept: Separate compute, storage, and data.

references.label: Choosing between relational and nonrelational data stores

title: Image-sharing architecture
prompt: For photo sharing, store originals, transform them on arrival, and search posts. Select 2 incorrect architectures.

choices.text: Store original photos in an IAM policy.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. An IAM policy defines permissions.

choices.text: Store original photos in S3.
choices.explanation: It can handle file contents as objects.

choices.text: Consider using Lambda to transform files when they arrive.
choices.explanation: It suits event-driven processing.

choices.text: Choose a database based on the post search requirements.
choices.explanation: Check the search method before choosing.

choices.text: Run an OS-resident service using S3 alone.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. S3 is not a compute environment.

learning.reason: Assign responsibilities by function.
learning.concept: S3, Lambda, and DB have different roles.

title: Selection Process
prompt: Choose two statements that are incorrect about the process for selecting services for a new feature.

choices.text: Identify who processes what and when.
choices.explanation: This clarifies the factors for deciding how to run it.

choices.text: Check how the data will be stored and searched.
choices.explanation: This is necessary for choosing storage and a database.

choices.text: Choose a service name you already know first, then fit the requirements to it later.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Break down the requirements first.

choices.text: Always make a single service handle every responsibility.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Consider combining services for each responsibility.

choices.text: Check each service’s permission boundaries as well.
choices.explanation: Separating responsibilities also clarifies the permissions required.

learning.reason: Follow the sequence from requirements to responsibilities.
learning.concept: Design by combining services.

title: Authentication
prompt: Choose one correct statement about authentication.

choices.text: Verify who the entity accessing the resource is.
choices.explanation: Authentication verifies the identity of a person or entity.

choices.text: Authorize operations on S3 objects.
choices.explanation: This is an authorization decision.

choices.text: Encrypt data.
choices.explanation: Encryption is a means of protecting data.

learning.reason: Distinguish between the two stages.
learning.concept: Authentication verifies the entity's identity.

title: Authorization Failure
prompt: After signing in, you received AccessDenied for a specific bucket. Choose the one correct first step to investigate.

choices.text: Check only the password entry screen.
choices.explanation: Because you are already signed in, this may not be an authentication-only problem.

choices.text: Check the requested operation, the target bucket, and the permission policies.
choices.explanation: For authorization, check the required action and resource.

choices.text: Change S3 to EBS.
choices.explanation: Changing the storage service does not help identify the cause of the denial.

learning.reason: After authentication, check authorization.
learning.concept: Authorization is specific to each operation.

title: Distinguishing the stages
prompt: You made multi-factor authentication mandatory at login. Choose the one correct judgment that considers both authentication and authorization.

choices.text: Verification of the principal is strengthened, but permissions for S3 operations continue to be managed by policies.
choices.explanation: Multi-factor authentication strengthens verification of the principal. Authorization determines what a verified principal is allowed to do.

choices.text: Passing multi-factor authentication makes it possible to read and write to every bucket.
choices.explanation: Stronger identity verification does not automatically add permissions to operate on resources.

choices.text: Because authentication has been strengthened, policies for the target resources are no longer needed.
choices.explanation: Authentication and authorization address different questions, so management of permissions for operations on targets remains necessary.

learning.reason: Distinguish between verifying who someone is with multi-factor authentication and deciding what that principal is allowed to do.
learning.concept: Even when authentication is strengthened, authorization for resources is still required separately.

title: Roles
prompt: Choose the one incorrect statement about IAM roles.

choices.text: An identity that grants permissions to the principal that assumes it.
choices.explanation: Attach permission policies to a role.

choices.text: Always has a long-term password and long-term access keys.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Roles do not have long-term credentials.

choices.text: AWS services can assume a role.
choices.explanation: Services such as EC2 can also use roles.

learning.reason: Understand the characteristics of roles.
learning.concept: A role is an identity that can be assumed.

title: EC2 Permissions
prompt: An application on EC2 writes to a specific S3 bucket. Select the one incorrect way to provide permissions.

choices.text: Attach a role to EC2 that has only the S3 actions required.
choices.explanation: Grant only the minimum permissions required to the role of the runtime environment.

choices.text: The application uses temporary credentials from the role.
choices.explanation: It can run without embedding long-term keys.

choices.text: Write a long-term access key directly into the source code.
choices.explanation: This is a method to avoid. It goes against the design of using a role and temporary credentials.

learning.reason: Pass runtime environment permissions through a role.
learning.concept: Do not embed long-term keys in the application.

title: Choosing a principal
prompt: Select one incorrect statement about principals and roles.

choices.text: Principals exist only for people using the console; applications running on EC2 have no actor.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. A principal is an entity that performs an action, and is not limited to people. Even for a request in which an application on EC2 uses a role's temporary credentials, authorization checks which principal is making the request.

choices.text: Grant permissions only after identifying which principal will perform the action.
choices.explanation: Identifying the principal is the starting point.

choices.text: Do not share the same long-term key between a person and a running application.
choices.explanation: You can assign separate roles to each principal and use temporary credentials.

learning.reason: Both people and running applications have principals; match each with appropriate credentials and permissions.
learning.concept: A principal is not limited to a person.

title: Explicit Deny
prompt: Choose two statements that are correct about IAM policy evaluation.

choices.text: An explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow.
choices.explanation: An explicit deny takes precedence during evaluation.

choices.text: Once you find one Allow, you do not need to check any other policies.
choices.explanation: Check Deny statements and conditions as well.

choices.text: Policies are unrelated to resources.
choices.explanation: Evaluate by specifying the action and resource.

choices.text: When investigating, specify the principal, action, and resource.
choices.explanation: Evaluate the request with its details fixed.

choices.text: Deny applies only to encryption.
choices.explanation: Deny is part of access permission evaluation.

learning.reason: Understand the evaluation order.
learning.concept: An explicit Deny takes precedence.

title: Investigating AccessDenied
prompt: A read is denied even though there is an Allow. Select 2 correct investigation steps.

choices.text: Grant administrator permissions without checking what the error concerns.
choices.explanation: This violates least privilege and does not reveal the cause.

choices.text: Check whether the requested action and resource match the Allow.
choices.explanation: This checks for a mismatch in the target.

choices.text: Delete and recreate S3.
choices.explanation: This does not investigate policy evaluation.

choices.text: Ignore Deny if the request is authenticated.
choices.explanation: An explicit Deny takes precedence.

choices.text: Check for an explicit Deny and conditions in the bucket policy and other policies.
choices.explanation: These can cause a denial even when there is an Allow.

learning.reason: Check both permissions and denials.
learning.concept: Investigate by specifying the target precisely.

title: Permission outcome
prompt: Both an Allow for S3:GetObject and an explicit Deny for the same target are present. Choose 2 correct judgments.

choices.text: The operation is denied.
choices.explanation: An explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow.

choices.text: It will always succeed because there is an Allow.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect because it ignores the Deny.

choices.text: Investigate the policy and conditions that cause the Deny.
choices.explanation: This is the next step to narrow down the cause.

choices.text: The Deny will disappear if you authenticate again.
choices.explanation: Repeating authentication does not remove a policy Deny.

choices.text: S3 does not evaluate policies.
choices.explanation: Access is evaluated through IAM and resource policies, among other mechanisms.

learning.reason: Apply precedence rules when there is a conflict.
learning.concept: Deny takes precedence.

title: Least privilege
prompt: Select the 2 statements that are incorrect about least privilege.

choices.text: Specify the required actions and resources.
choices.explanation: This is the starting point for narrowing the scope of access.

choices.text: To make things work, grant administrator permissions for all resources from the outset.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. First determine the required scope.

choices.text: Separate the required roles for each principal.
choices.explanation: People, CI, and applications can be separated.

choices.text: Share a single long-term access key among everyone and all applications.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. It undermines separation of principals and traceability.

choices.text: Review permissions based on actual usage.
choices.explanation: This helps determine how to reduce excessive permissions.

learning.reason: Avoid broad permissions.
learning.concept: Least privilege means limiting access to what is needed.

title: Daily job
prompt: Grant permissions to a daily CSV import job. Choose 2 incorrect methods.

choices.text: Always allow deletion from all buckets.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Limit permissions to the reads and writes that are needed.

choices.text: List the input and output bucket paths.
choices.explanation: You can specify the resources precisely.

choices.text: Give the job role only the operations it needs.
choices.explanation: This follows the principle of least privilege for the principal.

choices.text: Consider a role that can use temporary credentials.
choices.explanation: This can reduce the distribution of long-term keys.

choices.text: Copy a developer’s personal access key into the job configuration.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Separate personal credentials from the execution environment.

learning.reason: Narrow the scope to what the job requires.
learning.concept: Use roles and temporary security credentials.

title: Permission Design Sequence
prompt: Select two statements that are incorrect as approaches to designing permissions for a new process.

choices.text: List the actions the process performs and the resources they target.
choices.explanation: This is a prerequisite for least privilege.

choices.text: Assign separate roles to each execution principal.
choices.explanation: This clarifies permission boundaries.

choices.text: Allow all actions to avoid troubleshooting failures.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. It expands the scope of impact.

choices.text: Store long-lived keys with no expiration in shared configuration.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Consider temporary credentials.

choices.text: Verify actual access, including explicit denies and conditions.
choices.explanation: Confirm that only the intended scope is permitted.

learning.reason: Design permissions based on requirements.
learning.concept: Allow only the required scope.

title: In transit
prompt: Choose one correct statement about encryption in transit.

choices.text: Protects data moving across a communication channel.
choices.explanation: HTTPS/TLS is used to protect data in transit.

choices.text: Automatically encrypts stored disks.
choices.explanation: Encryption at rest must be configured separately.

choices.text: Makes IAM permissions unnecessary.
choices.explanation: Encryption and authorization are separate.
